# The Kettle

She had been standing at the window for an hour before anyone noticed. The kettle went cold on the counter, and nobody moved to fill it again. Outside, the street lamps came on one at a time, as if somebody were walking down the road and lighting them by hand. Her brother counted them aloud and lost his place at nine.

Nobody in the house said what they were waiting for. The telephone sat on its shelf by the stairs, and each of them had walked past it twice without looking. It was understood that whoever looked first would have to answer it.

By eight the soup had skinned over. Her mother ladled it out anyway and set the bowls down with a small, deliberate clatter, the sound of a woman insisting that this was still an ordinary evening. Nobody ate.

# The Thermostat

Her father had installed the thermostat himself the winter before, and he never trusted it. He would stand in the hallway and hold his palm flat against the wall, then read the little dial, then hold his palm to the wall again, as though the house might be lying to the machine.

The thermostat only knew one thing, which was the temperature of the hallway. It could not tell that the back bedroom was freezing or that the kitchen was stifling. It kept a single promise, to hold the hallway at nineteen degrees, and it kept that promise with total loyalty and no understanding.

She thought about this as she watched the lamps. A house can be perfectly regulated and still be a cold place to live in, because regulation measures what it was told to measure and nothing else.

# What the Telephone Said

When the telephone finally rang, it was her brother who crossed the room, because he was the only one who had stopped pretending not to wait. He listened for a long time. He said yes twice and no once, and then he put the receiver down so gently that it made no sound at all.

He turned around and looked at each of them in turn, and his face did the work that his voice could not. Her mother set down the ladle. Her father took his hand away from the wall.

The kettle was still cold. Nobody had noticed that either, and she crossed the kitchen and filled it, because it was the one thing in the room that she knew how to do.
